title: Testing Distributed Systems
subtitle: Watch one Orders service get tested with five kinds of test, from unit tests to injected network faults, and see what each layer catches.
learn: Why a test pyramid keeps most tests fast and few tests broad
How contract tests catch API drift between teams without a shared staging environment
Why integration tests should use a real database, not a mock
How a load test finds limits such as connection pool exhaustion
How to inject latency and failures to prove timeouts and fallbacks work

steps.title: Green tests, broken checkout
steps.body: Every unit test for the Orders service passes. Yet after deploy, checkout fails because the Payments team renamed a JSON field, and later a slow Payments call freezes the whole service. A single mocked function cannot reveal either problem. Distributed systems fail in the gaps between components, so tests must cover those gaps too.
steps.idea: Passing unit tests prove your code matches your assumptions, not that your assumptions are true.
steps.caption: Orders depends on a database and on Payments.

steps.title: Many fast unit tests
steps.body: The base of the pyramid is unit tests: pure logic such as price totals and state transitions, run in memory with no network. Take 1,200 of them at about 5 ms each, so a few seconds of test time plus about 30 s of build and startup, roughly 40 seconds in total. They are cheap, so run them on every commit and write lots of them. Above integration tests sit a handful of end-to-end tests that drive the whole system through its UI or public API: realistic but slow and flaky. The pyramid is a rule of thumb: the higher a layer, the slower, costlier and flakier it is, so keep fewer of them.
steps.idea: Put most tests where feedback is fastest and failures are easiest to diagnose.
steps.caption: Runner exercises Orders logic in memory.

steps.title: Contract tests for the API gap
steps.body: Orders is the consumer of the Payments API. Its tests record what it relies on, such as a POST /charges reply containing amount and status, and publish that contract to a broker. The Payments team's build downloads every consumer contract and verifies its real code against them. If Payments renames status, their build fails before release. No shared staging environment is needed.
steps.idea: A contract test catches breaking API changes at the provider's build, where they are cheapest to fix.
steps.caption: Orders publishes; Payments verifies in its build.

steps.title: Use the real database
steps.body: Next come integration tests with real dependencies. The runner starts a throwaway Postgres container (for example with Testcontainers), applies the real migrations, and runs 80 tests through the actual SQL. A mocked database would happily accept a query that violates a unique constraint, mistypes a column name, or relies on a migration you forgot to write. A real one does not. These tests cost about three minutes, so run them on every pull request, not every keystroke.
steps.idea: Stub remote services you do not control; run the infrastructure you own, such as your database, for real.
steps.caption: Orders runs real SQL against a container.

steps.title: Inject latency and failures
steps.body: Payments is stubbed behind a fault proxy that can delay, drop or error on command. The test makes Payments take 5 seconds, then asserts that Orders gives up after its 500 ms timeout and returns a clear 'try again' response instead of hanging. Without this test, the timeout code is untested and probably wrong. Other faults to try: connection reset, HTTP 503, duplicate delivery.
steps.idea: Failure-handling code only works if you have watched it run against a failure.
steps.caption: Proxy stalls Payments; Orders must time out.

steps.title: Load test the baseline
steps.body: A load generator now replays realistic traffic, say 500 requests per second for 10 minutes, against a production-like deployment. It measures latency percentiles, not averages, because the slowest 1 percent of requests is what users complain about. The healthy result here is p99 near 180 ms with errors below 0.1 percent. Save that as the baseline to compare against after every release.
steps.idea: Load tests produce a baseline; their value is comparing against it later.
steps.caption: 500 req/s through Orders and Postgres.

steps.title: Push past the limit
steps.body: Raise the rate to 1,500 requests per second. Assume each request holds a connection for about 20 ms, so 20 connections serve about 1,000 req/s. Beyond that the service uses up its 20 database connections, and the unserved third queues until requests time out. The p99 climbs to 2.4 seconds and about 30 percent of requests fail. No unit test could show this, because the limit comes from how pieces interact under concurrency. The fix might be faster queries, a pooler such as PgBouncer, a cache, or shedding load early; a bigger pool alone often just moves the queue to the database.
steps.idea: Load tests find the knee in the curve where queues build and latency explodes.
steps.caption: Pool exhausted at 1,500 req/s: about 30% of requests fail.

steps.title: Cost and flakiness
steps.body: Broad tests are expensive and can fail for reasons unrelated to your change: a slow CI machine, a shared environment, a clock race. A suite that fails randomly trains people to rerun and ignore it. Keep upper layers few, give each a clear purpose, make them deterministic with fixed seeds and no real sleeps, and quarantine flaky tests quickly. Production monitoring and gradual rollouts, covered in other lessons, catch what testing cannot.
steps.idea: A test suite is only useful if people trust a red result.
steps.caption: Each layer adds coverage and cost.

steps.title: Which layer catches what
steps.body: Five kinds of test, each aimed at a different risk. Unit tests guard logic, contract tests guard API agreements, integration tests with real dependencies guard SQL and wiring, fault injection guards timeouts and fallbacks, and load tests guard capacity. Many cheap tests at the bottom, a few expensive ones on top. Each layer answers a different question, so skipping one leaves that question open.
steps.idea: Match each risk to the cheapest test that can reveal it.
steps.caption: Five kinds of test, five different risks covered.

quiz.q: The Payments team renames a response field. Which test would fail in the Payments build before release?
options: A unit test inside Orders
A load test against Orders
A provider verification of Orders' published contract
A snapshot of the Orders database
quiz.why: The broker holds what Orders relies on. Payments verifies its real code against that contract, so the rename fails their build.

quiz.q: Why run integration tests against a real Postgres container instead of a mocked repository?
options: A real database enforces constraints, types and SQL syntax that a mock silently accepts
Mocks cannot be written for databases
Containers make tests run faster than unit tests
It removes the need for unit tests
quiz.why: A mock returns whatever you told it to, so bugs in the SQL or schema stay hidden. A real database rejects them.

quiz.q: A load test reports an average latency of 90 ms, yet users complain about slow checkouts. What should you check?
options: Only the maximum single request
The number of unit tests
Whether the load generator is a container
p95 and p99 percentiles, which show the slow tail
quiz.why: Averages hide the slow tail. A few percent of very slow requests barely move the mean but affect many real users.

quiz.q: A fault-injection test makes a dependency take 5 s, and Orders also hangs for 5 s. What does this reveal?
options: The dependency is healthy
The timeout is missing or misconfigured
The test pyramid is inverted
The contract is out of date
quiz.why: A correct client would stop waiting at its own timeout. Hanging for the full delay shows that protection is not working.

quiz.q: Your suite has few unit tests and thousands of browser-driven end-to-end tests, and it fails randomly. What is the best direction?
options: Add more end-to-end tests
Rerun failures until they pass
Move checks down to unit, contract and integration tests, and keep few end-to-end ones
Delete the integration tests
quiz.why: Lower layers are faster and more deterministic. Shifting coverage down gives quicker, more trustworthy feedback.

cheatsheet.def: Rule of thumb: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. Cost and flakiness rise with each layer.
Checks that a consumer's expectations of an API match what the provider actually returns, verified in the provider's build.
Start real dependencies such as Postgres or Kafka in disposable containers for each test run, then throw them away.
A stand-in (stub, mock, fake) for a dependency. Use for remote services you do not control or that are slow; run infrastructure you own, such as your database, for real.
Load test: expected traffic, to confirm the baseline. Stress test: push beyond it to find the breaking point.
p99 means 99 percent of requests were faster. Report percentiles, not averages, because users feel the tail.
Deliberately add delay, errors, drops or duplicates to a dependency to prove timeouts, retries and fallbacks behave.
A test that passes and fails without code changes. Fix or quarantine it fast; it erodes trust in the whole suite.
